assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row. Otherwise the assertion PASSES.
assertions.evidence: All three tables vary expectation columns across rows: Decision? ranges over AUTO_APPROVED/APPROVED/REJECTED; Premium? ranges over 0.00, 108.00, 112.00, 138.00, 221.00, 250.00, 277.00. No expectation is a verbatim copy of an input, and a fixed-value implementation would fail multiple rows.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone; (3) a helper method used in the assertion applies a comparison criterion (ordering, tolerance, subset matching) that is stated nowhere in the table, title, or description. Otherwise the assertion PASSES.
assertions.evidence: @Description in `rejectsApplicationsAboveRiskThreshold` states 'Risk score = (age / 10) + (claimCount * 15)' and 'exceeds 75', exposing internal formula and threshold. Per spec: 'the risk score is internal...must not appear...in @Description — the reader sees its effect through the input/output rows, not the arithmetic.'

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails.
assertions.evidence: All three method names state system behaviour: 'autoApprovesRenewalsWithNoClaimsRegardlessOfAge' (what the code does), 'rejectsApplicationsAboveRiskThreshold' (what the code does), 'calculatesPremiumBySeniorAgeTier' (what the code does). Striking 'the system' leaves no true external fact.
